opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting case, and honestly a pretty rational one when you look at where Xiaomi sits. They're not just a phone company anymore. They have phones, a huge consumer IoT ecosystem, and now cars. If you believe AI is going to be the interface layer across all of those devices, then depending entirely on someone else's model is a strategic vulnerability. So building in-house capability makes a lot of sense.

On the model side, what I've found notable is that Chinese companies broadly have gotten very good at training strong models efficiently, and many of them have embraced open weights. That creates a healthy ecosystem where a company like Xiaomi can hire talented researchers, build on shared knowledge, and get to a competitive model faster than you'd expect. They don't need the single best frontier model in the world. They need models that are good, cheap to serve, and deeply integrated into their products, especially smaller models that can run on-device. That's a different optimization target than chasing the top of a leaderboard.

The hardware ambition is the harder part. Designing your own chips is a long, expensive grind, and the export control environment makes access to cutting-edge manufacturing and compute genuinely constrained for Chinese companies. But there's a long-term logic: if you control the silicon, the model, and the device, you can co-design them and get efficiency gains a model-only company can't. Apple is the obvious template, and Xiaomi clearly sees itself in that mold.

My main caution is focus. Training competitive models takes sustained investment in data, post-training, and evaluation, not just a big pretraining run. Lots of companies announce models and then fall behind in six months because the field moves so fast. Whether Xiaomi treats this as a core, permanent capability or a marketing moment will decide how it plays out. But directionally, I think more vertically integrated players building their own AI stacks is where the industry is heading, and Xiaomi is well positioned to try.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will be the interface layer across Xiaomi’s phones, IoT devices, and cars, and that vertically integrated AI stacks are where the industry is heading.

r002.rationale: It presents Xiaomi’s in-house models, chips, and devices as part of a broader industry shift toward vertically integrated AI stacks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Xiaomi is one of the most interesting cases to watch, because they're coming at this from a direction that almost none of the Western labs can. They're not an AI company that's trying to figure out distribution. They're a company that already ships hundreds of millions of phones, plus cars now, plus every category of home device you can imagine, and they're asking, "What does it mean for us to own the model layer too?"

On the model side, I'd be honest that they're a few steps behind the frontier. The MiMo releases were a real signal, though. Those were reasonably competitive open-weight models at the small and mid sizes, and the fact that they published them openly tells you something about the strategy. They're not trying to win the benchmark race against DeepSeek or Qwen head on. They're trying to be good enough on-device and at the edge, where latency, cost, and privacy matter more than the last few points on a math eval. For a hardware company, that's actually the right bet. You don't need the best model in the world to make a phone assistant feel dramatically better. You need a model that's tightly integrated with the OS, the camera, the car, and all the sensors you already control.

The hardware ambition is the part that I think people underrate. Building your own silicon for inference is incredibly hard, and the Chinese ecosystem has a huge incentive to do it because of export controls. If you're Xiaomi, you can't assume you'll always have access to the latest Nvidia parts. So vertical integration isn't a vanity project, it's a hedge. And Xiaomi has a track record of grinding on hardware margins that most software companies simply don't have the patience for.

Where I'm more skeptical is on the frontier training side. Training truly state-of-the-art models is a capital and talent game, and right now in China that talent is concentrated at a handful of places. Xiaomi is spending to attract it, but there's a real question of whether a consumer electronics company can sustain the kind of research culture that produces breakthroughs rather than fast followers. My guess is they don't need to. They need to be a very good adopter and fine-tuner of open models, including other people's, and own the deployment surface.

So I'd frame it this way: Xiaomi probably won't be the lab that defines the next paradigm. But they might be one of the companies that defines what everyday AI actually looks like for a billion users, because they control the devices those users touch all day. That's a different kind of power, and in the long run it may matter just as much.

r001.rationale: The response describes integrating Xiaomi’s models with its devices and services, but does not predict that AI will become more deeply integrated into digital technologies broadly.

r002.rationale: It characterizes Xiaomi’s vertical integration as a strategic hedge, but does not present the ambition as an example of a broader tendency among large companies to build everything in-house.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing about Xiaomi is that they already have a way to put AI into people’s hands. They have phones, they have devices in the home, and they have cars. So building their own models could give them more control over how those products work together, what runs locally, and what needs to go to the cloud.

But I’d separate the ambition to build models from the need to have the best model in the world. Those are different goals. You could build a very successful AI product with a model that’s optimized for your hardware and your users, even if it isn’t leading every benchmark.

The challenge is execution. Having a model and having hardware doesn’t automatically produce a good experience. The question is whether they can make AI reliably useful in things people already do. That’s where I’d look to judge the strategy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI across Xiaomi’s phones, home devices, and cars, but does not predict that AI will become increasingly integrated into digital technologies broadly.

r002.rationale: It discusses Xiaomi building its own models and having hardware, but does not characterize this as a broader tendency for large companies to build everything in-house.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing about Xiaomi is that they have a lot of ways to put AI in front of people—phones, cars, devices around the home. So the question is how much owning the model helps them build a better experience across those products.

There’s a pretty strong argument for having that capability internally. You can make choices about latency, privacy, and what runs on the device versus in the cloud. If you’re designing the hardware too, you can optimize those things together.

But building models is expensive, and having a huge hardware business doesn’t automatically make you good at model research. I’d look at whether they can turn that investment into features people actually use. They don’t necessarily need the best model on every benchmark. They need models that work really well for the products they’re shipping.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI across Xiaomi phones, cars, and home devices, but does not predict that AI will become increasingly integrated into digital technologies broadly.

r002.rationale: It discusses Xiaomi building models and designing hardware, but does not frame this as an example of a broader tendency among large companies to build everything in-house.
